1:
Gill explains the name before the command. Abib, sometimes called Nisan, answered to part of our March and part of April, and took its name from the corn then appearing in the ear and beginning to ripen, when all things were in their verdure; the Greek translators simply called it the month of new fruit. It was appointed the first of the months for sacred purposes, and it was the month in which Israel came out of Egypt and the first passover was kept, which is what makes it a month to be taken notice of. Wesley says the same in a line, adding that the change of the year's beginning was made by a special order from God in remembrance of the deliverance; Henry notes that before this the year had been reckoned to begin in September. Henry also draws out the force of the command to observe the month when only one week of it was festival: their preparation beforehand, and their reflection upon it and improvement of it afterwards, were to be so serious as to amount to an observance of the whole month. Keil and Delitzsch call it simply the earing month, and observe that the precise day is not fixed here because it was already known from the account in Exodus.

Why the deliverance is dated to the night is disputed. Wesley takes it straightforwardly: it was in the night that Pharaoh was forced to give them leave to depart, so that they made their preparations then and perfected the work in the morning. Henry reports that the Chaldee paraphrasts would not have it so, since there was an express order that no one should stir out of doors till morning, and they therefore render the clause as meaning that Israel came out of Egypt by daylight — one of them expanding it as he brought thee out of Egypt, and did wonders by night, the other as and thou shalt eat the passover by night. Clarke supplies the reason for the feast's name from the same night: the destroying angel, seeing the blood of the appointed sacrifice sprinkled on the lintels and door-posts of the Israelites' houses, passed over them and did not destroy any of their firstborn.

Keil and Delitzsch warn that the phrase rendered keep the passover is being stretched here. It is used primarily of preparing the paschal lamb for a festal meal, but is employed in this passage in a wider sense, so that passover covers not the lamb only but the paschal sacrifices generally — what the rabbins gather under the common name chagiga — meaning all the sacrifices slain during the seven days of unleavened bread, though not the burnt-offerings and sin-offerings prescribed elsewhere for the feast. Henry reaches the same conclusion by a different road, noting that the passover was itself a sacrifice, which is why Christ our passover is said to be sacrificed for us, and that no sacrifice was accepted except from the altar that sanctified it. Calvin looks past the mechanics to the purpose. He has already treated the institution under the First Commandment, since the Passover was a symbol of redemption in which the people exercised themselves in the pure worship of the one God, acknowledging him as their only Father and distinguishing him from every idol; and he presses what follows from the single sanctuary — one altar was prescribed for them, as if God would gather them under one banner for the preservation of concord and the unity of the faith.
2:
Gill fixes the time from the tradition: the fourteenth day of Abib at night, between the two evenings, as the Targum of Jonathan has it — the very hour at which Israel came out of Egypt — and he takes the lamb to be a type of Christ, the passover sacrificed for us. That raises the first difficulty, since the command is to sacrifice the passover of the flock and the herd, though the paschal victim was a lamb or a kid only. Wesley resolves it by widening the noun: the word stands for the feast of the passover as a whole, so that the clause may be rendered thou shalt observe the feast of the passover unto the LORD thy God, with sheep and with oxen, as the sacrifices appointed for those days elsewhere require. On where it was to be done, Gill glosses within any of thy gates as the cities, so named because they commonly had gates in which public business was transacted, and notes that in none but Jerusalem might the passover be killed and eaten. The place where God would set his name he understands of the ark and the mercy seat with the cherubim over them, where God caused his divine Majesty to dwell — Jerusalem, once Solomon had built the temple.

The bread is called the bread of affliction, and the three witnesses divide over which affliction is meant. Clarke takes it of the bondage: baked without leaven it was unsavoury, and its very taste put them in mind of their afflictive servitude in Egypt. Calvin takes it of the escape instead. By this sign they were reminded of having got away in haste, as it were out of the very flames, and their recollection is to be carried back to the straits they were rescued from — for they must have been in the greatest extremity when there was no time even to bake bread; so the loaf is called the bread of affliction in order that the manner of the deliverance may the more enhance God's grace. Wesley will have both, saying it was bread neither usual nor pleasant, to remind them at once of the miseries they endured in Egypt and of the hurry of their coming out, which left no time to leaven or prepare it. Gill adds what the prohibition came to in practice: before the feast they searched every room in the house, and every hole and crevice, that none might remain.

Three smaller cruxes close the section. Wesley gives three reasons why the killing was confined to the sanctuary — that so great a work might be done with the solemnity God required; that this was a sacrifice and not a sacrament only, with the sprinkling of blood that is the essential part of one; and that it might mark out the place where Christ, the true passover, was to be slain. On the command to roast, Gill concedes that the Hebrew word properly signifies to boil, and that Onkelos so renders it, yet boiling the paschal lamb is expressly forbidden. Some therefore refer the verse to the chagigah and the other offerings of the feast, and Gill notes that in Josiah's day the passover was roasted with fire while the other holy offerings were boiled in pots and pans and divided quickly among the people; but the connection with the preceding verses seems to him to mean the lamb, and he follows Jarchi in taking the word of roasting with fire despite its form. The arithmetic of the last verse divides Gill from Wesley. Gill holds that unleavened bread was eaten on the seventh day as on the others, that day being set apart only for its own special service; Wesley solves the sum differently, counting the six days as those besides the first, on which the passover was killed.
9:
Gill sets out the reckoning plainly: seven weeks were to be numbered, and then a second feast fell due, called from the counting the feast of weeks and sometimes Pentecost, from its being the fiftieth day. Calvin fits it into the agricultural year. The Passover had fallen when the harvests were just beginning to ripen, and the firstfruits were offered then; seven weeks later came this second festival, which the Greeks named from the fifty. Calvin adds a coincidence he thinks worth marking — that exactly this number of days lay between the departure of the people from Egypt and the publication of the Law. At the later feast another offering of firstfruits was made, in which each man consecrated a gift to God from the harvested produce according to his ability and in proportion to what the year had yielded; and to make them readier and more cheerful in that liberality, God's blessing is set before them, as though Moses were commanding the people to testify their gratitude, since whatever springs out of the earth is the mere bounty of God himself. Wesley notes that the tribute asked was over and besides what had already been appointed, and Gill observes that it was at this same feast, long afterwards, that the Spirit was poured out upon the apostles.

The command to rejoice is what Calvin dwells on, and he treats it as an argument rather than a mood. God exhorts them to willingness on the ground that his service brings this rejoicing with it, and nothing ought to stimulate us to obedience more than knowing that God consults our good rather than seeking any advantage from us. Calvin grants at once that ungodly men rejoice too — indeed they are wanton and intemperate in their joy — but since that joy is transient and their laughter is turned into weeping and gnashing of teeth, Moses is right to magnify this other kind as a peculiar blessing: to rejoice before God, as if a father should invite his children to delight themselves together with him. By so external an exercise believers were being taught that there is no real or desirable joy except in reference to God; and however the wicked abandon themselves to their pleasures, tranquillity of conscience, which alone brings true rejoicing, is wanting to them, so that they do not actually enjoy the merriment they plunge into. Gill describes the same command from the outside: make a liberal feast and keep it cheerfully in the presence of God, in the place where he dwells, thankfully acknowledging all his mercies and favours.

Clarke explains what such rejoicing looked like in practice — the offerings were to be eaten with festivity, shared with friends liberally and bestowed on the poor with great generosity, so that these too might partake of the meal with joy before the Lord. He then accounts for a related rule in a strikingly plain way: to answer those ends the flesh had to be eaten while fresh, since in that climate putrefaction soon set in, which is why nothing was to be left until the morning. That consideration, Clarke says, is sufficient by itself to account for the command, without having recourse to the moral and evangelical reasons the learned and devout Ainsworth assigned to it; and he borrows Harmer's exclamation at how beneficent and cheerful the design of the whole institution is. The section ends by turning the celebrants back toward Egypt. Calvin reads that as an amplification by comparison, the recollection of a most miserable captivity being introduced to heighten the sweetness of their present condition; Gill draws the practical conclusion, that remembering they had been bondmen and were now delivered should make them liberal in the freewill offering, generous in the feast they provided, and compassionate toward the stranger, the widow and the fatherless.
13:
Gill dates the third festival to the fifteenth of Tisri, answering to our September. Calvin explains why that month was chosen, and the reasoning is economic as much as liturgical. The first day was called the day of In-gathering, because by then the produce of the whole year had been stored in the granaries and provision cellars; and since the people were at that point resting from their rural labours, it was a convenient season for a festival. Calvin presses the point further: it was so arranged by God precisely in order that they might go up to Jerusalem more willingly, the journey costing them little expense and little sacrifice of their domestic interests. The command is therefore fitted to the year's work rather than imposed across it, and the same consideration that made the harvest a reason for gratitude also made it the moment at which a week away from home was affordable.

What Keil and Delitzsch draw out is who the rejoicing includes. The law here simply enforces the observance of the feast at the central sanctuary and exhorts the people to rejoice at it — but the exhortation is not left to the household head and his own children. He is to allow not only his sons and daughters a share in that joy but the manservant and the maidservant too, together with the portionless Levites and the strangers among them. Gill describes the character of the celebration rather than its guest list: it was kept at the ingathering of the fruits of the earth in token of gratitude and thankfulness for the goodness of God bestowed upon them, and he notes that the Targum of Jonathan adds the flute and the pipe, instrumental music being used to increase the joy of the occasion.

Calvin then takes up the closing words of the section, and finds a promise hidden inside what reads as a command. Where our version has when the LORD shall have blessed thee, the Hebrew stands literally as because he shall bless thee, and though the sense is nearly the same, the change of conjunction matters: Moses is assuring them that if they devote their minds diligently and faithfully to God's service they will never want grounds for rejoicing, since he will never interrupt the flow of his blessing. So the end of the verse is not a mere command but also a promise — if they were not ungrateful, there was no fear but that God would continually supply new cause for gladness, the two clauses running together as God will bless thee, and therefore thou shalt only rejoice. Calvin weighs the small particle carefully, allowing that it may properly mean nevertheless but noting that it equally bears the sense of however, at any rate, or truly. His own rendering is only joyful, and not sad: there was to be no sorrow or anxiety admitted that might hinder them from the gladness the day required.
16:
Gill notices that this requirement has already been given elsewhere and asks why it should be repeated, and his answer explains the shape of the whole chapter. It is set down again for the sake of naming the place at which they were to appear, which the earlier statements had not specified; indeed, Gill says, it is chiefly for that reason that the other festivals have been recited here at all. Keil and Delitzsch describe the repetition the same way — the law that the men appear before the Lord three times a year at the three feasts just mentioned, now carrying the additional clause at the place which the LORD shall choose, together with an explanation of what it means not to appear empty, namely that every man is to bring according to his gift. Ellicott adds the detail that in the parallel passage a promise is attached which does not appear here: that their land should be safe while they were away from it.

Calvin asks who was actually bound by the command, and answers with a series of concessions to human weakness. Although the other feast-days were not to be neglected, God would make some allowance for the infirmity of his people, and so did not impose the necessity of going up to Jerusalem five times in the year; and because only the first half of the seventh month contained three of the feast-days, the same consideration meant that it was required of the males alone to leave their houses for the sacred convocations. The women are thereby spared, Calvin says, travelling being less convenient for them — and besides, through the fruitfulness God had promised them they were almost always either pregnant or nursing. He reckons boys and young men under twenty excepted as well, since the term males takes in only those who were comprised in the census.

That raises an objection Calvin states himself: in the spiritual worship of God there is no difference between male and female, so why should the obligation fall on one sex? The reply, he says, is easy. The fathers of families presented themselves at the sanctuary in the names of their wives and children, so that the profession made there was extended to the other sex and to those of tender age; and he hears David alluding to the same thing when he sings of a people who come with voluntary offerings in the day of thy assembly, in the beauties of holiness, seeking, after the manner of the prophets, an example of freewill offering from the legal worship. A second objection Calvin finds already anticipated in the law itself: lest the Jews should protest that stripping the land of its defenders by gathering every man into one place invited invasion, God had promised that he would see to it that no one should so much as desire to assail their forsaken homes. On the size of the gift, Gill observes that the law fixes no quantity — the wise men appointed one afterwards, but the Lord left it to the generosity of the people, laying down only the general rule that each should give according to his ability and as God had prospered him. Jarchi puts the same rule concretely: every man who has many eatables and much goods shall bring many burnt offerings and many peace offerings.
18:
Two offices are named, and the witnesses labour to distinguish them. Gill, following Maimonides, places the judges in the court of judicature and describes the officers as masters of the staff and the whip, who go out into the markets and streets and shops to regulate weights and measures and to smite all who do wrong — everything they do being by order of the judges. Clarke reaches for English equivalents: the first are much what our magistrates or justices of the peace are, the second like our inquest sergeants and beadles, who entered houses and shops to examine weights and measures and the conduct of the people, and brought an offender before the magistrate to be punished on the spot; Clarke notes they seem also to have served as heralds in the army, and observes that in China all minor offences are still punished on the spot in the magistrate's presence. Keil and Delitzsch put the office higher. The word means literally writers, and these men were not merely messengers and servants of the courts but secretaries and advisers of the judges, named from their duty of keeping the genealogical lists, and already existing in Egypt. Wesley describes them as subordinates who brought causes before the judge, made his sentence known, and carried it out.

Who appoints them is genuinely disputed. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the nation is addressed as a whole and directed to appoint judges for itself — to choose them and have them inducted by its rulers, as at Sinai, where the people chose and Moses installed — and they add the sharp caution that election by majorities was unknown to the Mosaic law. Calvin grants the privilege was real but denies it is a universal rule: it is not conceded to all peoples to elect their judges, God having honoured his chosen people with that prerogative, and what the passage recommends generally is regular government rather than any one method. Whether magistrates come by the suffrages of the people or are imposed in some other way, Calvin says, they are the necessary ministers of God to confine all men under the yoke of the laws — for public utility is what makes their authority agreeable, which it would otherwise be hateful. Henry is content to leave the method open in the same way: however the persons were pitched upon, whether by the appointment of their sovereign or the election of the people, the power was ordained of God. Ellicott notes that a fresh synagogue section opens here, the land now being considered as the seat of the Kingdom of Jehovah. Henry and Wesley agree on the later shape of the system: a court of twenty-three judges in every town of more than a hundred and twenty families, and a court of three in the smaller ones.

The charge laid on them is exacting. Henry states the standard bluntly — better not judge at all than not judge with just judgment — and turns the closing command into a series of demands: adhere to the principles of justice, act by its rules, countenance its demands, imitate its patterns, and pursue with resolution whatever appears to be just. Wesley explains why the bribe is singled out: a gift biasses the mind so that a man cannot discern between right and wrong, and it works even on judges accustomed to righteous dealing. Gill renders the doubled word strictly — justice, justice, and nothing else — and Calvin explains what the emphatic repetition is for. It inculcates that judges should study equity with inflexible constancy, and not without cause, since nothing is more likely to happen than that men's minds should be clouded by favour or by hatred; and besides that, there are so many quibbles by which justice is perverted that unless judges watch very cautiously against deception they will often find themselves ensnared.
21:
Gill is careful to say what is not forbidden. The prohibition covers trees of any sort, oaks or any other, but it was never unlawful to plant trees or even groves of them — only to plant them for a religious or idolatrous use. Wesley gives the reason in a line: this was the practice of idolaters, and might be an occasion of reviving idolatry. Calvin sets it in the wider religious world and treats it as a rule of separation. Among the heathen nations groves were sacred, so that with them no religious object could receive due reverence except under the shade of trees; and lest conformity with so general a custom should vitiate the pure worship of God, this distinction was drawn. The intent of the prohibition, Calvin says, is that the Jews should fly from all strange rites, in case by approaching the Gentiles too closely they should introduce a sinful medley. That it was needed appears from how eagerly they imitated the nations anyway — there was scarcely any period in which they abstained from the high places, and it is not without reason that Isaiah and Jeremiah reproach them for playing the harlot under every green tree.

Clarke and Ellicott converge independently on a different reason, and it is about visibility rather than separation. Clarke observes that groves were planted about the idol temples for the sake of the obscene worship performed in them, and that on this account God would have no groves or thickets about his own altar, so that there might be no room even for the suspicion that anything contrary to the strictest purity was transacted there — every part of the divine worship being publicly performed, for the purpose of general edification. Ellicott says the same in a sentence: the worship of Jehovah allowed of no secret rites, and nothing that might lead toward the abominations of heathen idolatry could be permitted near the altar. He adds a philological note, that the Hebrew word is sometimes used of images but is here evidently used of the grove itself.

The second prohibition raises a genuine difficulty. Gill defines the term as a statue or pillar set up for idolatry, and reports Aben Ezra's important qualification: what was not set up for idolatry was not forbidden at all, as when a stone was erected in memory of some action or remarkable event. Keil and Delitzsch identify it more narrowly still as a memorial stone or stone pillar dedicated to Baal, and Ellicott passes on Rashi's explanation of it as a single stone, whether statue or pillar. Calvin faces the contradiction head on. God elsewhere commands that stones be erected on the borders of the land with the sum of the Law inscribed upon them; at first sight the two commands collide, and Calvin grants they would, unless the statue meant here is understood as a false image of God in which men set him before themselves in bodily form — which is why the clause that God hates such things is attached. He then makes a small grammatical choice with a large result, referring the relative pronoun not to the image that is set up but to the act of setting it up, so that what the sentence declares abominable is the erecting itself. The reason follows: by that act God's glory is dishonoured, when he is transfigured into a body, or when anything corporeal is mixed with his spiritual nature.
